title: Weekly Top Five Articles: A World Worth Tending
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley's weekly curated digest opens with the thought that what people deem significant shapes or warps who they are, and that what gives lives weight is diminishing. He summarizes five pieces: Benjamin Paul Myers on Robert Frost's spiritual apathy, B. D. McClay on envy as a vice of mirrors, a PsyPost report that strong social networks predict higher fertility than generous welfare, research linking a belief that the world lacks meaning to willingness to endorse political violence, and a study of how peer, academic and family problems interact with autism and ADHD traits in Japanese students. Each entry adds Bradley's own interpretive line on why it matters. He ties the five together as evidence that people are formed by what they attend to and who is allowed to care for them. This is a Pass A archive of the roundup itself, and the linked pieces were not expanded.
points: McClay argues envy is a vice of mirrors that social media monetizes, and that it resists self-laceration but is vulnerable to laughter.
A Finnish study of 100,750 adults found that community social support predicted birth rates regardless of economic status, even where welfare is generous.
Research led by Daniel Snook found low belief that most things and people matter was the strongest predictor of willingness toward violent extremism.
Photographing things that matter reduced violent intentions in the study, possibly by helping people see meaning in more places.
Bradley's synthesis is that attention and attachment form the inner life, and when they weaken, apathy, comparison, grievance and fear follow.
quotes: Opening thought: what we deem significant fundamentally molds or warps who we are as persons. What gives our lives weight is slowly diminishing.

B. D. McClay argues that envy, “pain over the good fortune of others and a corresponding pleasure over their misfortunes,” is a vice of mirrors that compromises “our judgements and our aspirations, shrinking and distorting our interior world.
The big idea: “getting married and having kids is a deeply social decision”: folks are happy to have children when they know somebody who will help shoulder the burden.
My interpretation: Violence is rationalized when the bodies in the street (or elsewhere) would seem smaller.
What it means: your child’ mental pain and his outside social world aren’t two discreet spheres but make up a single developmental ecology.
We are made by attention and attachment: what we notice as worthy of care, and who we allow to care for us when we fail.
